pages.text:
1 
 
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
 
 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
Docket No. ER26-3380-000 
MOTION TO INTERVENE AND REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION,  
OR IN THE ALTERNATIVE, LIMITED PROTEST OF  
TRACT HOLDING COMPANY I, LLC 
Pursuant to Rules 211, 212, and 214 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal 
Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”),1 Tract Holding Company I, LLC 
(“Tract”) hereby submits this motion to intervene and request for clarification of, or in the 
alternative, limited protest to, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) proposed Reliability 
Backstop Procurement (“RBP”) framework, filed in the above-captioned proceeding on July 31, 
2026,2 pursuant to Section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”).3 
For the reasons set forth below, Tract respectfully requests that PJM clarify the scope of 
“executed electric service agreement[s] or transmission service agreement[s]” that new load may 
present as evidence of Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW.4 Absent such clarification, the 
Commission should find that PJM has failed to satisfy its burden under Section 205 of the FPA 
and should sever and reject the relevant portion of PJM’s proposed tariff revisions as unduly 
discriminatory or preferential, and direct modifications consistent with the Commission’s 
authority under NRG Power Marketing, LLC v. FERC, 862 F.3d 108 (D.C. Cir. 2017).5 
 
1 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.211, 385.212, 385.214. 
2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource Adequacy Concerns 
Stemming from Large Loads, Docket No. ER26-3380-000 (filed July 31, 2026) (“PJM RBP Filing”). 
3 16 U.S.C. § 824d. 
4 PJM RBP Filing at 39-40; Proposed PJM Tariff, Attachment DD, §§ 18.2(c)(i)-(iii). 
5 NRG Power Mktg., LLC v. FERC, 862 F.3d 108 (D.C. Cir. 2017). Whereas here, PJM has consented to any 
modifications to the RBP filing, the D.C. Circuit “has held that . . . the Commission has ‘authority to propose

2 
 
I. 
MOTION TO INTERVENE 
Tract respectfully moves to intervene in this proceeding.6 Tract, through its affiliates, 
acquires land and develops shovel-ready development sites for data centers in the PJM region—
pre-positioning power, fiber, zoning and entitlements, and will be directly subject to PJM’s RBP 
process should the Commission accept PJM’s filing. Tract therefore has a substantial and direct 
interest in the outcome of this proceeding that cannot be adequately represented by any other party. 
Accordingly, Tract requests that the Commission grant this motion, consistent with the public 
interest. 
II. 
COMMUNICATIONS 
Please address all notices and communications regarding this proceeding to the following 
persons who are also designated for service in this proceeding. 
Orijit Ghoshal 
Vice President, Government and 
Regulatory Affairs  
Allison Girvin 
Vice President and Corporate Counsel  
3200 E Cherry Creek South Drive 
Suite 700  
Denver, CO 80209  
Tel: 406-202-4519 
orijit.ghoshal@tract.com              
allison.girvin@tractcapital.com   
Tyler O’Connor 
Kathy Lowrey 
Crowell & Moring LLP 
600 Fifth St NW 
Washington, D.C. 20001 
Tel: 202-624-2704 
klowrey@crowell.com  
toconnor@crowell.com 
 
 
 
 
 
III. 
BACKGROUND  
The instant proceeding concerns proposed revisions to the PJM Tariff and Reliability 
Assurance Agreement to institute the RBP, a “one-time, supplementary mechanism to procure 
 
modifications to a utility’s [FPA section 205] proposal.’” See, e.g., N.Y. Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 188 FERC ¶ 
61,051, at P 22 n.36 (2024) (alteration in original) (citing NRG Power Mktg., 862 F.3d at 114-15); see Midcontinent 
Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 180 FERC ¶ 61,141, at P 26 n.29 (2022), order on reh’g, 182 FERC ¶ 61,096 (2023); 
ISO New Eng. Inc., 175 FERC ¶ 61,172, at P 16 n.20 (2021).  
6 18 C.F.R. § 385.214.

3 
 
additional supply to meet the resource adequacy needs of the PJM Region.”7 Following the 
2027/2028 base residual auction clearing 5.6% short of PJM’s target reserve margin, on January 
16, 2026, the PJM Board initiated a Critical Issue Fast Path Process (“CIFP”) to address PJM’s 
resource adequacy challenges.8 
Following the conclusion of the CIFP, on July 31, 2026, PJM submitted the instant filing 
to establish what it characterizes as a “critical safety net designed to address current resource 
adequacy shortfalls” observed in the base residual auctions for the 2028/2029 delivery year.9 
According to PJM, the RBP “will only procure the capacity necessary to cover any remaining 
shortfall from the 2028/2029 BRA after PJM has accounted for new capacity being brought by 
new load or that otherwise qualify for a limited opt-out from the RBP.”10 Tract generally supports 
and commends PJM addressing the BRA shortfall by requiring loads to either curtail, bring their 
own capacity, or enter the RBP. 
Under PJM’s proposal, “new capacity voluntarily brought on to the PJM system by new 
load” that satisfies the criteria set forth in proposed tariff section 18.2 may be credited as 
Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW, thereby reducing the Initial RBP Target.11 In addition, new 
load that participates as Annual Demand Resources or DER Capacity Aggregation Resources may 
also reduce the Initial RBP Target.12 These new capacity and curtailment offset options are 
required under the Statement of Principles Regarding PJM issued on January 16, 2026, by the 
 
7 PJM RBP Filing at 7. 
8 David E. Mills, PJM Board Chair, Board Decisional Letter on Critical Issue Fast Path - Large Load Additions, 
PJM Board (Jan. 16, 2026), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/who-we-are/public-
disclosures/2026/20260116-pjm-board-letter-re-results-of-the-cifp-process-large-load-additions.pdf.  
9 PJM RBP Filing at 26. 
10 Id. 
11 See id. at 35, 39. 
12 Id. at 40.

4 
 
National Energy Dominance Council (“NEDC”) and the 13 governors of the PJM states.13 
However, proposed section 18.2(c) requires that new load present an “executed electric service 
agreement or transmission service agreement” demonstrating that such load will achieve 
commercial operation within the applicable delivery year in order for the Qualifying RBP Offset 
UCAP MW or Annual Demand Resources or DER Capacity Aggregation Resources to decrement 
the Initial RBP Target.14 This evidentiary requirement warrants clarification. 
IV. 
REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION 
A. 
PJM Should Clarify the Scope of Agreements Load Can Provide As Evidence 
of Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW and Annual Demand Resources or 
DER Capacity Aggregation Resources. 
Tract respectfully requests that PJM clarify that the undefined terms “electric service 
agreement and transmission service agreement” encompass executed agreements with load serving 
entities or transmission owners that evidence a binding commitment by new load to achieve 
commercial operation by or during the relevant delivery year. As currently drafted, the proposed 
tariff language is not clear whether functionally equivalent agreements that serve the same 
evidentiary purpose as electric and transmission service agreements would satisfy the Qualifying 
RBP Offset UCAP MW or Annual Demand Resources or DER Capacity Aggregation Resources 
eligibility requirements set forth in section 18.2(c). Absent such clarification, PJM risks 
understating the volume of legitimately committed new load that will achieve commercial 
operation by or during the relevant delivery year and that satisfies the requirements for Qualifying 
RBP Offset UCAP MWs or Annual Demand Resources or DER Capacity Aggregation Resources, 
thereby inflating the Final RBP Target beyond that necessary to address any actual resource 
 
13 Statement of Principles Regarding PJM, National Energy Dominance Council, 1 (Jan. 16, 2026), 
https://www.energy.gov/documents/statement-principles-regarding-pjm (urging PJM to allow loads to not be 
allocated RBP costs if they “self-procured new capacity or agreed to be curtailable”). 
14 PJM RBP Filing at 39-40; Proposed PJM Tariff, Attachment DD, §§ 18.2(c)(i)-(iii).

5 
 
adequacy shortfall. This result would be inconsistent with the NEDC’s and Governors’ Principles 
and outside the control of the load who may be subject to EDC tariffs and rules that do not 
contemplate the named agreements. 
As drafted, the requirement for load to provide an executed electric or transmission service 
agreement serves an evidentiary function: to “indicat[e] that the load will be coming online” in the 
relevant delivery year.15 The requirement screens out speculative load and ensures that only load 
that has assumed binding obligations sufficient to demonstrate it will achieve commercial 
operation within the applicable timeframe may be credited as Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW 
or Annual Demand Resources or DER Capacity Aggregation Resources. While electric service 
and transmission service agreements satisfy that standard, other executed agreements—including 
transmission security agreements and construction letters of authorization—impose binding 
commitments equally probative of genuine load commitment. That some EDCs either do not 
utilize those agreements or do not require loads coming online in the 2028/2029 delivery year to 
execute them so far in advance does not make such loads any less likely to reach commercial 
operation. Of course, such loads must demonstrate some evidence of commitment to come online, 
and the Commission should find that transmission security agreements and construction letters of 
authorization suffice. 
The Commission has recently accepted executed transmission security agreements filed by 
Commonwealth Edison Company (“ComEd”) and PECO Energy Company (“PECO”), two 
transmission owners in PJM.16 ComEd and PECO utilize these agreements to govern the terms 
 
15 PJM RBP Filing at 39-40; Proposed PJM Tariff, Attachment DD, §§ 18.2(c)(i)-(ii). 
16 See, e.g., Commonwealth Edison Company, 196 FERC ¶ 61,040 (2026); Commonwealth Edison Company, 196 
FERC ¶ 61,042 (2026); PECO Energy Company, 195 FERC ¶ 61,074 (2026); PECO Energy Company, 193 FERC ¶ 
61,148 (2025).

6 
 
under which they provide retail electric delivery services to large load customers that will not take 
transmission service under PJM’s tariff.17 As the Commission explained in its order accepting 
ComEd’s executed transmission security agreement with Tract’s affiliate, Grundy County Power 
NR I, LLC (“GCP”), the agreement imposes binding financial commitments designed to ensure 
the data center achieves commercial operation on schedule: 
ComEd states that the Transmission Security Agreement establishes protections in 
the event of GCP’s failure to timely construct the Data Center and related facilities, 
failure of such facilities to reach commercial operation by the commercial operation 
date, 
failure 
to 
remain 
in 
operation 
throughout 
the 
term 
of 
the Transmission Security Agreement, or failure to operate in conformance with 
the agreed upon load phasing schedule (Load and Phasing Schedule) for a given 
year.18 
Similarly, the construction letter of authorization that Tract’s other affiliate has executed 
with Virginia Electric and Power Company (“Dominion”), authorizes Dominion to commence 
engineering, procurement, and installation of the facilities and associated equipment required to 
provide electrical service to its forthcoming data center project and imposes binding obligations 
on the executing party including equipment deposits and payments owed for delay or project 
cancellation. That neither ComEd nor Dominion have tendered electric service agreements or 
transmission service agreements for these two projects that are otherwise contractually committed 
to achieve commercial operation during the 2028/2029 delivery year should not preclude the 
projects from securing their own capacity and thereby satisfying the evidentiary requirements for 
Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW and Annual Demand Resources or DER Capacity Aggregation 
Resources. Even those electric distribution companies that execute electric service agreements 
 
17 PECO Energy Company, 193 FERC ¶ 61,148 at P 2 (2025). 
18 Commonwealth Edison Company, 194 FERC ¶ 61,181 at P 3 (2026).

7 
 
with large loads often do not tender them until 12 months in advance of energization.19 Requiring 
large loads to demonstrate evidence of such agreements now—rather than transmission security 
agreements or construction letters of authorization agreements—would functionally prevent large 
loads with commercial operation dates in the 2028/2029 delivery year from meeting the 
requirements for Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW or Annual Demand Resources or DER 
Capacity Aggregation Resources, in violation of the NEDC’s and Governors’ Principle to allow 
loads that procure their own capacity or agree to curtail to avoid being double-counted in the 
auction. 
Like electric and transmission service agreements, both transmission security agreements 
and construction letters of authorization impose binding commitments on developers and EDCs20 
to bring a project online within a defined timeframe and impose material financial consequences 
on a developer that fails to satisfy its obligations. PJM should therefore afford sufficient flexibility 
in evaluating the agreements that new load may present as evidence of Qualifying RBP Offset 
UCAP MW or Annual Demand Resources or DER Capacity Aggregation Resources—including 
transmission security agreements, construction letters of authorization, and functionally equivalent 
instruments—to ensure that the RBP process accurately accounts for all genuinely committed new 
load that is properly matched with new supply. The Commission has accepted proposals that afford 
precisely such flexibility in other contexts.21 
 
19 Application of Virginia Electric and Power Company for Approval of its Large-Load Connection Queue Process 
Standards, Case No. PUR-2026-00011, at 74 (Va. State Corp. Comm’n Apr. 15, 2026) (explaining the Dominion 
“offers Electric Service Agreements to customers approximately one year before energization of service”). 
20 For instance, Dominion’s construction letter of authorization authorizes Dominion to install the facilities 
necessary to provide electric service. 
21 Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., 192 FERC ¶ 61,064 at P 208 (2025) (accepting MISO’s 
proposal to allow applicants to provide “other agreements” to satisfy a showing of an executed agreement with load 
and explaining it “provides considerable flexibility . . . to satisfy this requirement”).

8 
 
Absent clarification from PJM, a narrow interpretation of “electric service agreement and 
transmission service agreement” risks producing the very outcome PJM sought to avoid: load 
paying to procure capacity in the RBP that could otherwise be served by its own capacity or 
through curtailment.22 Such a result would directly contravene the stated purpose of the RBP—to 
institute “a one-time mechanism that will only procure the capacity necessary to cover any 
remaining shortfall from the 2028/2029 BRA after PJM has accounted for new capacity being 
brought by new load or that otherwise qualify for a limited opt-out from the RBP.”23 
V. 
LIMITED PROTEST 
A. 
To The Extent Not Clarified As Argued Above, PJM’s RBP Filing Is Unduly 
Discriminatory Because It Excludes Similarly Situated New Loads From 
Eligibility For Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW and Annual Demand 
Resources or DER Capacity Aggregation Resources. 
The Commission has long held that a rate, term, or condition is unduly discriminatory 
where it treats similarly situated customers differently absent a legitimate basis for doing so.24 
Should PJM decline to provide the requested clarification, the Commission should reject the RBP 
filing as unduly discriminatory or preferential under Section 205 of the FPA.25  
By restricting the types of executed agreements new loads may present to obtain eligibility 
for Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW and Annual Demand Resources or DER Capacity 
Aggregation Resources, PJM’s proposal draws an impermissible distinction among similarly 
 
22 PJM RBP Filing at 37-38.  
23 Id. at 26 (emphasis added).  
24 See El Paso Nat. Gas Co. Aera Energy, LLC, 104 FERC ¶ 61,045 at P 115 (2003), reh’g denied, 106 FERC ¶ 
61,233 (2004) (“Discrimination is undue when there is a difference in rates or services among similarly situated 
customers that is not justified by some legitimate factor.”). 
25 See 16 U.S.C. § 824d(b); See Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 193 FERC ¶ 61,171 at P 91 (2025) (the applicant “bear[s] the 
burden of demonstrating that proposed tariff revisions are . . . not unduly discriminatory or preferential.”).

9 
 
situated customers.26 As explained above, new load customers that have executed transmission 
security agreements, construction letters of authorization, or similar agreements have undertaken 
binding contractual and financial commitments functionally equivalent to those assumed under 
standard electric service or transmission service agreements. In each case, the customer has 
demonstrated a genuine, non-speculative commitment to achieve commercial operation within a 
defined timeframe; the sole relevant distinction lies in the particular contractual instrument through 
which that commitment has been formalized. PJM’s proposal permits the latter category of 
customers to qualify for RBP offset eligibility while denying the former any opportunity to do so, 
without any reasoned justification for the disparate treatment.27 
This discrimination is particularly impactful in this instance because large load customers, 
such as data centers, by virtue of their scale and operational characteristics, are often subject to 
non-standard contractual instruments before being tendered electric or transmission service 
agreements. As explained above, electric distribution companies are increasingly requiring data 
centers to execute bespoke instruments—such as transmission security agreements and 
construction letters of authorization—which impose substantial financial commitments at least as 
probative of genuine load commitment as a standard electric or transmission service agreement. 
PJM’s proposal thus creates a discriminatory preference for customers whose agreements bear a 
 
26 See Transmission Agency of N. Cal. v. FERC, 628 F.3d 538, 551 (D.C. Cir. 2010) (explaining that the 
Commission cannot treat similarly situated entities differently (citing Sacramento Mun. Util. Dist. v. FERC, 474 
F.3d 797, 802 (D.C. Cir. 2007)). 
27 See, e.g., id.; N.Y. Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 162 FERC ¶ 61,124, at P 10 (2018) (“To say that entities are 
similarly situated does not mean that there are no differences between them; rather, it means that there are no 
differences that are material to the inquiry at hand.”).

10 
 
particular label, while penalizing those who have undertaken equivalent binding commitments to 
demonstrate their load is real, committed, and coming online within the relevant delivery years.28 
Given that PJM has acknowledged the requirements of Section 18.2(c) are intended to 
demonstrate that interconnecting load will achieve commercial operation within the applicable 
delivery year, the Commission should condition acceptance of the RBP filing on PJM’s submission 
of revised tariff language permitting PJM to evaluate whether any executed agreement evidences 
a genuine, binding commitment to achieve commercial operation within the applicable delivery 
year.29 For example, PJM could adopt the following revisions, shown in red, to proposed tariff 
section 18.2(c)(i)-(iii): 
(i) Signed bilateral contracts for Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW for at least five 
Delivery Years with a commercial operation date prior to the start of the 2032/2033 
Delivery Year, and matched with load that has an executed electric service agreement, or 
transmission service agreement or any other binding agreement, indicating that the load 
will be coming online in the 2027/2028 or 2028/2029 Delivery Year; 
 
(ii) Self-Supply generation that is in a Relevant Electric Retail Regulatory Authority 
(“RERRA”)-approved or accepted integrated resource plan with either associated 
generation in the PJM interconnection queue or signed bilateral contracts for Qualifying 
RBP Offset UCAP MW for at least five Delivery Years with a commercial operation date 
prior to the start of the 2032/2033 Delivery Year, and matched with load that has an 
executed electric service agreement, or transmission service agreement or any other 
binding agreement, indicating that the load will be coming online in the 2027/2028 or 
2028/2029 Delivery Year; or   
 
(iii) Signed commitment between a Curtailment Service Provider or DER Aggregator and 
new load(s) that has an executed electric service agreement, or transmission service 
agreement or any other binding agreement, indicating that the new load(s) will, in a MW 
quantity equal to MW quantity of the new load(s), either (a) participate as Annual Demand 
Resources or DER Capacity Aggregation Resources starting in the 2028/2029 Delivery 
Year Second Incremental Auction and continuing through the 2032/2033 Delivery Year, 
or (b) purchase replacement Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW that are eligible generation 
or storage resources.  
 
28 See PacifiCorp, 171 FERC ¶ 61,112 at PP 100-102 (2020) (rejecting a proposal where similarly situated 
customers were required to make different showings of commercial readiness). 
29 Commission may take such action because PJM has consented to the Commission’s exercise of authority to 
modify or sever elements of the RBP filing. See NRG Power Mktg., LLC v. FERC, 862 F.3d 108 (D.C. Cir. 2017).

11 
 
 
Absent such modification, PJM’s proposal will arbitrarily foreclose Qualifying RBP Offset 
UCAP MW and Annual Demand Resources or DER Capacity Aggregation Resources eligibility 
for an entire class of similarly situated new load customers—a result that is neither just nor 
reasonable, nor consistent with the prohibition against undue discrimination under the FPA. 
VI. 
CONCLUSION 
For the foregoing reasons, Tract respectfully requests that PJM provide the clarification 
requested herein, or, in the alternative, that the Commission sever and reject the relevant portion 
of PJM’s RBP filing as unduly discriminatory and direct PJM to submit revised tariff language on 
compliance consistent with this filing. 
 
 
Respectfully submitted, 
 
 
 
 
 
 
August 21, 2026
